Emirates saw H1 profits slide 66% on Iran war impact

Federico Maccioni, Joanna Plucinska | Reuters News

Emirates, the Middle East's largest airline, is seeing strong demand on routes to China, Russia and Africa, but feeling the squeeze from high fuel prices linked to the Iran war, its President Tim Clark told Reuters on Wednesday.

The Dubai-based carrier reported a 66% drop in first-half net profit this month after airspace closures and disruptions caused by the nearly nine-month conflict hit travel across the Middle East and drove up oil and jet fuel prices.

Dubai International Airport said on Tuesday that passenger traffic fell 28.1% in the first nine months of the year, although it added that traffic was recovering.

Brent crude traded as high as $120 a barrel earlier this year, but has eased to about $93 in recent weeks on hopes of de-escalation.

"The industry needs to have oil back at $70," Clark said in an interview at his office in Dubai International. "That's the rate in which people can trade. The global economy will move, the airline industry will be in a better place."

Clark said that higher costs could trigger bankruptcies across the airline sector, though added that state-owned Emirates remained profitable despite narrower margins.

"We managed to make money in the first half. Not bad at all, given fuel is the level it is, that's the real kicker," Clark said. "It's fuel, not people. We're filling the airplanes."

Gulf carriers have gradually restored operations, but recent attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have clouded prospects for a full recovery.

STRONG DEMAND FROM RUSSIA, CHINA, AFRICA

Emirates said this month it had restored operations across 91% of its network by the end of September. Its passenger seat factor, a measure of how many seats are filled, fell to 72% in the first half from 79.5% a year earlier.

Clark said strong traffic on some routes was helping to offset weakness elsewhere.

"It's very strong. If you look at the Russian market, you look at the some of the African points that we're serving. Look at Asia, China is full," he said, adding meanwhile that Oceania "needs a little bit of help".

The Emirates Group had 54.1 billion dirhams ($14.7 billion) of cash at the end of September, down 5.5 billion dirhams from six months earlier as it drew on reserves to support operations.

Clark said the company was closely monitoring cash flow but remained "in good shape" and had no immediate need to raise debt.

"Now if something adverse happens, we will recourse to the debt markets. But at the moment, we're not there," he said.

Clark also said there were no plans for an initial public offering of the airline and that any decision on a listing rested with the Dubai government.

"At the enterprise value level, we are, I would say, probably in about $120, $130 billion if you look at the multiples of EBITDA," he said, adding that a listing could raise significant proceeds.

"It's a question they (the government) have asked themselves in the past. I don't think with any degree of seriousness."

($1 = 3.6725 UAE dirham)

(Reporting by Federico Maccioni and Joanna Plucinska in Dubai. Editing by Adam Jourdan and Mark Potter)
